ABSTRACT



Background.

Third-generation

cephalosporin

(3GCR)

and

carbapenem-resistant

(CR)

Enterobacterales

are

classified

as

critical

priority

pathogens

by

the

World

Health

Organization

(WHO).

We

assessed

the

total

and

direct

effects

of

third-generation

cephalosporin

and

carbapenem

resistance

on

30-day

mortality

in

Enterobacter

cloacae

complex

(Ecc)

bloodstream

infections

(BSIs).

Methods.

We

conducted

a

retrospective

multicenter

cohort

study

including

patients

with

healthcare-associated

Ecc

BSIs

from

four

hospitals

in

Brazil

(2012–2023).

Isolates

were

classified

into

three

WHO

resistance

profile

groups:

profile

1,

susceptible

to

both

third-generation

cephalosporins

and

carbapenems;

profile

2,

3GCR,

susceptible

to

carbapenems;

and

profile

3,

CR.The

primary

outcome

was

30-day

mortality.

A

hierarchical

Cox

proportional

hazards

model

was

used

to

sequentially

adjust

for

baseline

characteristics,

clinical

severity,

and

treatment-related

variables,

allowing

assessment

of

mediators.

Results.

Overall,

97

of

429

patients

(22.6%)

died

within

30

days

of

BSI

onset.

Thirty-day

mortality

was

20.6%

(62/300)

in

WHO

profile

1,

25.2%

(26/103)

in

profile

2,

and

34.6%

(9/26)

in

profile

3

(
p

=

0.20).

In

the

final

model,

WHO

resistance

profiles

were

not

independently

associated

with

mortality

(profile

2:

adjusted

hazard

ratio

[aHR],

0.75;

95%

confidence

interval

[CI],

0.46–1.23;

profile

3:

aHR,

0.63;

95%

CI,

0.29–1.32).

Sequential

adjustment

progressively

attenuated

the

crude

associations,

with

greater

impact

of

baseline

patient

characteristics

among

profile

3

infections

and

of

treatment-related

variables

among

profile

2

infections.

Conclusions.

In

Ecc

BSIs,

antimicrobial

resistance

did

not

exert

a

direct

effect

on

mortality

after

accounting

for

key

mediators.

The

increased

mortality

observed

in

carbapenem-resistant

Ecc

BSIs

reflects

indirect

effects

operating

through

patient

baseline

status,

illness

severity,

and

treatment-related

factors.

ABSTRACT



Background.

Third-generation

cephalosporin

(3GCR)

and

carbapenem-resistant

(CR)

Enterobacterales

are

classified

as

critical

priority

pathogens

by

the

World

Health

Organization

(WHO).

We

assessed

the

total

and

direct

effects

of

third-generation

cephalosporin

and

carbapenem

resistance

on

30-day

mortality

in

Enterobacter

cloacae

complex

(Ecc)

bloodstream

infections

(BSIs).

Methods.

We

conducted

a

retrospective

multicenter

cohort

study

including

patients

with

healthcare-associated

Ecc

BSIs

from

four

hospitals

in

Brazil

(2012–2023).

Isolates

were

classified

into

three

WHO

resistance

profile

groups:

profile

1,

susceptible

to

both

third-generation

cephalosporins

and

carbapenems;

profile

2,

3GCR,

susceptible

to

carbapenems;

and

profile

3,

CR.The

primary

outcome

was

30-day

mortality.

A

hierarchical

Cox

proportional

hazards

model

was

used

to

sequentially

adjust

for

baseline

characteristics,

clinical

severity,

and

treatment-related

variables,

allowing

assessment

of

mediators.

Results.

Overall,

97

of

429

patients

(22.6%)

died

within

30

days

of

BSI

onset.

Thirty-day

mortality

was

20.6%

(62/300)

in

WHO

profile

1,

25.2%

(26/103)

in

profile

2,

and

34.6%

(9/26)

in

profile

3

(
p

=

0.20).

In

the

final

model,

WHO

resistance

profiles

were

not

independently

associated

with

mortality

(profile

2:

adjusted

hazard

ratio

[aHR],

0.75;

95%

confidence

interval

[CI],

0.46–1.23;

profile

3:

aHR,

0.63;

95%

CI,

0.29–1.32).

Sequential

adjustment

progressively

attenuated

the

crude

associations,

with

greater

impact

of

baseline

patient

characteristics

among

profile

3

infections

and

of

treatment-related

variables

among

profile

2

infections.

Conclusions.

In

Ecc

BSIs,

antimicrobial

resistance

did

not

exert

a

direct

effect

on

mortality

after

accounting

for

key

mediators.

The

increased

mortality

observed

in

carbapenem-resistant

Ecc

BSIs

reflects

indirect

effects

operating

through

patient

baseline

status,

illness

severity,

and

treatment-related

factors.
